objectives: Describe the structure of a machine instruction
Explain immediate, direct and indirect addressing
reviewNotes: The instruction set is an invented teaching set (clearly stated); the Board will use its own instruction set (e.g. a Little Man Computer style or a real CPU). Replace the mnemonics after checking the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Instruction format
blocks.md: A machine instruction has an **opcode** (the operation) and an **operand** (the data or the address of the data). The instruction set is the list of instructions a CPU understands. **Assembly language** uses mnemonics such as LDA (load) or ADD instead of binary opcodes; an **assembler** converts it to machine code, one assembly line to one machine instruction. The instruction set below is a **teaching set invented for this lesson**, not a real CPU.

blocks.title: Addressing modes
blocks.md: **Immediate**: the operand is the value itself (LDI 5 puts 5 in the accumulator). **Direct**: the operand is the memory address of the value (LDA 20 loads the contents of address 20). **Indirect**: the operand is the address of a memory location that **holds the address** of the data. Immediate is fastest; indirect allows pointer-like access.

blocks.caption: A trace table of a four-line program that adds x and y and stores the result in z.
blocks.alt: Trace of LDA x, ADD y, STA z, HLT with accumulator values 12, 42, 42, 42.

blocks.title: Teaching instruction set
blocks.md: LDI n: ACC = n. LDA a: ACC = memory[a]. STA a: memory[a] = ACC. ADD a: ACC = ACC + memory[a]. SUB a: ACC = ACC - memory[a]. JMP k: PC = k. BRZ k: if ACC = 0 then PC = k. HLT: stop. Trace by writing the PC, instruction, ACC and memory after each line.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Confusing the operand value with an address (immediate vs direct).
- Forgetting that the PC already points to the next instruction while the current one executes.
- Assuming assembly is portable: each CPU family has its own instruction set.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Trace
blocks.statement: Memory: x = 12, y = 30. Program: LDA x; ADD y; STA z; HLT. What is stored in z?
steps: LDA x gives ACC = 12. ADD y gives ACC = 12 + 30 = 42.
STA z writes 42 to z; HLT stops.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Addressing modes
blocks.statement: Memory address 20 holds 35 and address 35 holds 8. What does ACC contain after (a) LDI 20, (b) LDA 20, (c) an indirect load using address 20?
steps: (a) Immediate: ACC = 20 itself. (b) Direct: ACC = memory[20] = 35.
(c) Indirect: memory[20] = 35 is an address; ACC = memory[35] = 8.

objectives: Convert a normalised floating-point number to denary
Convert a denary number to floating point
Explain precision, range and rounding errors
reviewNotes: Floating-point format is an assumed teaching format (8-bit two's complement mantissa with point after first bit, 4-bit exponent). The Board may use a different size; all worked examples verified in Python.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Mantissa and exponent
blocks.md: A **floating-point** number is stored as a **mantissa** (the significant digits) and an **exponent** (the power of 2), like scientific notation. Value = mantissa x 2^exponent. In this lesson: an 8-bit mantissa in two's complement with the binary point after the first bit (value from -1 to just under +1) and a 4-bit two's complement exponent. **Real formats (such as the IEEE standard) differ**; the Board will state its own format.

blocks.title: Normalised form
blocks.md: A positive mantissa is **normalised** when it starts 0.1 (between 0.5 and 1); a negative one starts 1.0. Normalising uses all the bits for precision: shift the mantissa left until it starts 01 or 10 and reduce the exponent by the same number of places.

blocks.caption: Eight mantissa bits 01101000 in blue and four exponent bits 0011 in orange, giving 6.5.
blocks.alt: Floating-point layout: mantissa 01101000 and exponent 0011 equal 6.5.

blocks.title: Converting to denary
blocks.md: Example: mantissa 0.1101000, exponent 0011. Mantissa = 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.0625 = 0.8125; exponent = 3, so the value = 0.8125 x 2^3 = 6.5. Moving the binary point 3 places right gives 110.1 = 6.5, the same.

blocks.title: Range and precision
blocks.md: More **mantissa bits** give more **precision** (more accurate values); more **exponent bits** give a wider **range**. With a fixed total size, one is traded for the other. Some decimals (like 0.1) have no exact finite binary form, so they are stored with a small **rounding error**; comparing floats with = can fail.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting that the exponent is two's complement and can be negative.
- Leaving a positive mantissa as 0.01... when it could be normalised.
- Believing floating point stores every decimal exactly.

exercises.prompt: Explain why 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point, and give one consequence.
exercises.model: In binary 0.1 is a recurring fraction (0.000110011...), so only an approximation can be stored. Consequence: calculations such as 0.1 + 0.2 may not equal 0.3 exactly, so equality tests on floats are unreliable.
